Meeting and talking to boaters and learning who they are and where they come from. Everyone has a cool story.

content:Speaker user says: Given the text: Northwest Youth Sailing - Start Sailing!
Like other youth sports and activities, sailing is meant to be fun, empowering, and social. Sailing offers a unique medium to teach more than just practical skills. Sailing can offer tranquility, adventure, and excitement all in one day. Adversity and challenges along the way provide many opportunities for personal growth and teamwork. Boating and water safety is a key component in every junior sailing program. These lessons are widely applicable to other types of boating and recreation.
Why Learn in a Small Boat?
Jack London once quipped that the "small boat sailor is the real sailor." Small sailboats are very responsive to weight placement, sail trim, and rudder movements. Those who master sailing a small boat develop exceptional feel and awareness. It's no wonder that most of the professional sailors in the America's Cup or Volvo Round the World Race started in 8' Optimist dinghies. The skills learned on a small boat are easily transferable to larger sailboats, while adults who learned on larger boats often find dinghy sailing very challenging.
There are about 50 learn to sail programs in Washington and Oregon. Sailing classes are taught by a variety of different organizations. Historically yacht clubs were the hub of youth sailing activities. Today a wide range of organizations are involved in sailing instruction. These range from independent non-profit sailing centers to commercial sailing schools, and even parks and recreation departments. Our geography has endowed us with many wonderful lakes, rivers, and protected harbors that are well suited to sailing instruction.
When it comes to Learn to Sail classes, community sailing centers and yacht clubs have a lot in common. Just like community sailing centers, yacht clubs offer junior sailing classes that are open to the public, though yacht club members may receive a discounted price. Because both employ instructors trained by US Sailing, the activities, curriculum, and quality of instruction between yacht clubs and community based programs is very similar. Your child can have a great experience at either a community sailing center or yacht club program. The key to any outstanding program is that it's safe, fun, and that the students are learning.
Learning to Sail is not expensive, or at least no more so than any other day camp, recreational class, or club sport activity. Community sailing centers are generally a little more affordable. For a 40-hour course, the cost is typically around $300-400. When you break that down, most programs cost between $7.50-$10.00 per hour of class time. That's cheaper than a baby sitter!
Many community sailing programs and yacht clubs offer scholarships for sailors to attend class. The criteria vary from program to program, but most believe that financial circumstance is no reason to miss out. In support of this, The Sailing Foundation grants scholarships for youth sailors in Washington and Oregon who qualify for the Free/Reduced Lunch Program.
What is a Learn to Sail Program Like?
Qualified instructors, good equipment, diverse class offerings, and affordability will make your experience a positive one. Proximity is usually the main reason for choosing a program, but aside from convenience there are some other factors you should carefully consider.
1) Does the Program Hire US Sailing Certified Instructors?
US Sailing Certified Level One Instructors have to pass a rigorous course through US Sailing which is the national governing body of sailing. Having a certified instructor means they have met national standards in safety, instruction, and are familiar with the US Sailing Curriculum. Certified instructors must also hold valid CPR/First Aid certs and a state approved boating license.
2) What's after Learn to Sail?
Programs tend to be either recreational or racing in nature. The first couple years of sailing are spent working on the fundamentals, but after a child masters the basics there are many paths from which to choose. Larger keel boats, STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, & Math) education, adventure sailing, boat building, windsurfing, or paddle sports are just a few examples of recreational pathways after Learn to Sail. It's good to know what opportunities exist after mastering the basics. The best programs offer multiple classes, pathways, and levels to keep sailors engaged and on the water.
3) Do They Offer Year-Round Programming and Activities?
Most smaller programs only operate during the summer months. Others offer year round programming such as weekend "Learn to Sail," race teams, high school sailing, or open sailing. If you want to keep your child on the water during the school year ask what they have to offer in the off-season. Being able to sail 8 or 10 months a year is a huge benefit! Your child won't have to "restart" every summer and will retain more of what they learned.
4) Are They Affiliated with a Local High School or College Team?
Partnering with a local high school or university can add a wealth of vitality to a program. Having high school and college sailors around means that there is a strong dinghy sailing culture, a qualified pool of knowledgeable instructors, and activities happening throughout the year. There are also opportunities for your child to be mentored by these athletes and one day go on to sail in high school or college themselves.

Pictures showed Ajax fans clashing with Greek police and at least two supporters being left bloodied.
Eleven people were "hospitalized" with minor injuries, a police spokesman told AFP.
"AEK FC unreservedly and by all means condemns the incidents of violence that took place ... Not only because they happened during a match for [the] UEFA Champions League, but also because they insult the long history of our club," said a statement on the Greek club's website.

UEFA has opened disciplinary proceedings against both clubs, while Ajax is yet to comment.
Ajax defender Matthijs de Ligt tried to calm things down ahead of the Group E contest. Firecrackers then went off in the second half.
Disturbances in Greek stadiums are nothing new.
In March the country's Superleague was temporarily suspended when PAOK owner Ivan Savvidis entered the pitch with a gun in the late stages of his team's 0-0 draw against AEK. A PAOK goal had just been disallowed for offside.
He later received a three-year ban from football and PAOK was docked three points.

Progressing in Europe's top club competition was made more impressive because Ajax -- which won the last of its four titles in 1995 -- had to go through three rounds of qualifying and has long sold its best performers.

"We're playing against a side of champions and the difference can be seen when they score with their first chance," Roma manager Eusebio Di Francesco was quoted as saying by UEFA.

An underlying position is that we are always in some state or another, whether it is happiness, confusion of whatever. Hypnosis is just another position, and just like happiness and other states, we can be guided into it by other people.
The state hypnotist thus uses methods such as progressive relaxation to guide the person into a deeper and deeper state of hypnosis. They basically believe that anyone can be equally hypnotised and it the only limiting factor is the skill of the hypnotist.
Trait theorists argue that not everyone can be hypnotised, and that some easily fall into a trance whilst others seem unable (or unwilling) to succumb.
The trait hypnotists will therefore start with a test of hypnotisability and may reject people who do not score sufficiently highly on this test. This is a typical action of a stage hypnotist who does not want to spend hours on the induction.

content:Speaker assistant says: The state and trait schools of thought differ in their approach to inducing hypnosis because they have different beliefs about the nature of hypnosis and how it is best induced.

The state school of thought believes that hypnosis is a particular state of consciousness that can be induced with a series of techniques such as progressive relaxation or guided imagery. In this approach, the hypnotist attempts to guide the subject into a deeper and deeper level of relaxation, allowing them to enter a trance state. The state school assumes that anyone is capable of being hypnotized, and the variations in hypnotic susceptibility depend on the hypnotist's skill and the subject's degree of responsiveness.

In contrast, the trait school of thought assumes that hypnosis is a characteristic or trait that varies among individuals. Trait theorists believe that some people are more suggestible and responsive to hypnosis than others, and they use techniques to identify these individuals. They approach hypnosis with a more selective method, testing individuals for their susceptibility to hypnosis, and then tailoring hypnosis induction techniques for that specific individual.

Trait hypnotists will use a range of methods to determine how susceptible an individual is, such as the hand-clasping test, eye fixation, arm rigidity, and others. Those who exhibit more suggestibility are more likely to hypnotize successfully, and the techniques used to induce hypnosis will be matched to their particular characteristics.

Thus, the state school of thought takes an approach in which the hypnotist imposes his techniques to induce a specific state, whereas the trait school first assesses the hypnotisability of the individual being hypnotized and then tailors the approach accordingly to maximize hypnosis' effectiveness. context:Day 51, 00:00 keywords: hypnosis, state school, trait school tags: communication, individual, techniques

content:Speaker assistant says: As a child, I was always afraid of water. I couldn't swim, and the mere thought of being in deep water was enough to make me break out in a cold sweat. So, when my friends invited me to go on a beach vacation with them, I was hesitant. I knew it would be a challenge, but I also knew that I couldn't let my fear control me.

The day we arrived, my friends rushed into the water, laughing and splashing about. I hesitated at the edge of the shore, taking hesitant steps forward until the water reached my knees. Suddenly, I was knocked down by a wave, and I panicked. I struggled to stand up, grabbing onto anything I could find, including my friends, who tried to get me to relax and enjoy the water.

Over the next few days, I watched as my friends swam and played in the water, having a great time. I sat on the beach, too scared to join them. And then one day, I decided enough was enough. I was tired of missing out on life because of my fear.

I took swimming lessons, learned how to tread water, and slowly started making progress. I practiced in the shallow end of the pool, then ventured into deeper water cautiously. With the help and encouragement of my friends, I started to overcome my fears little by little.

By the end of the trip, I was swimming confidently in the waves, enjoying the water just as much as my friends. I had overcome my phobia and gained a newfound sense of confidence in myself. I learned that facing my fears wasn't easy, but it was worth it. I realized that I had missed out on so much in life because of my fear, and I didn't want to let it control me any longer.

As I returned home, the lessons I learned stayed with me. I was more willing to take risks and try new things. I found myself living more in the present rather than worrying about the future or dwelling on the past. I also became an advocate for facing your fears, encouraging others to push past their own limitations.

Overcoming my fear of water was just one challenge that I faced in my life, but the lessons I learned from that experience have stayed with me. Today, I am more confident and willing to try new things. I know that by facing my fears head-on, I can live a more fulfilling and rewarding life. context:learning to swim keywords: fear, water, fear of water, overcoming fear, confidence, swimming, lessons, challenge, life tags: confidence, progress

content:Speaker assistant says: Of course! As I started to tackle my fear of water, I had to take it slow and steady. I found that going at my own pace and not pushing myself too hard was crucial in building my confidence. Here are some of the specific steps I took:

1. Swimming Lessons: Taking swimming lessons was a critical first step for me. They gave me a foundation of basic skills and helped me understand how to stay afloat and move through the water safely. With the help of a trained instructor, I learned different strokes, how to properly breathe when swimming, and how to tread water.

2. Breathing Exercises: Breathing exercises were a huge help whenever I felt panicked, nervous, or out of breath in the water. I took slow, deep breaths and focused on exhaling slowly to calm myself down. Practicing these breathing exercises in the pool helped me develop a sense of control and calmness.

3. Gradual Progression: I took baby steps in the water. I started with the shallow end of the pool and gradually made my way into deeper water. Each time I swam, I challenged myself to go a bit further or tread water for a bit longer. I also practiced in different pools or bodies of water to gain confidence in various settings.

4. Visualizations: Visualizing myself successfully swimming and enjoying the water helped me overcome my fear. Before going to swim each time, I would close my eyes and picture myself confidently swimming through the water. Visualizing success made it feel possible for me.

5. Positive Reinforcement: Celebrating small successes was important for me. For example, when I treading water for an extra minute, I would congratulate myself mentally. Positive self-talk and affirmations helped me to keep going and build confidence.

By taking these steps, I was gradually able to overcome my fear of water. Over time, the fear that had once consumed me was replaced by a sense of wonder and joy in the water. content:Speaker assistant says: 1. Stick to a consistent sleep schedule: Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends.

2. Create a sleep-conducive environment: Make sure your bedroom is quiet, cool, dark, and comfortable. Keep electronic devices out of the room or use blue light-blocking glasses if you must use them before bed.

3. Limit caffeine and alcohol: Avoid consuming caffeine or alcohol, especially in the evening.

4. Relax before bedtime: Develop a relaxing bedtime routine that helps you wind down, such as reading a book, taking a warm bath or practicing relaxation techniques.

5. Avoid late-night meals and snacks: Eating late at night can interfere with sleep quality, try to eat large meals earlier in the evening.

6. Exercise: Regular exercise can improve sleep quality, but avoid exercising too close to bedtime.

7. Manage stress: Stress and anxiety can disrupt sleep, find ways to manage stress such as yoga, meditation, or talking to a therapist.

8. Consider melatonin supplements: In some cases, melatonin supplements may help improve sleep quality, although it's always best to speak with a healthcare provider before taking them.

9. Get enough sunlight: Expose yourself to natural light during the day for better circadian rhythms and sleep-wake cycles. 

10. If you're having trouble sleeping or have a sleep disorder that's impacting your daily life, talk to your doctor about the best treatment options for you. context:new context keywords: sleep, schedule, environment; tags: sleep, schedule, environment, stress
